item.title: What Male Friendship Actually Sounds Like
item.description:
Friends

What Male Friendship Actually Sounds Like

How podcasts can shed light on how male friendships develop, mature, and thrive.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Random banter is an essential part of keeping male friendships alive.
  • A regular place to show up and be seen supports lasting bonds.
  • Joking around and busting each others chops helps men bond.
Before We Record Magic
Source: Abdellah Benziane / Pexels

Podcasts are one of my favorite things to be on (and listen to). The reason is simple.

Before hitting record, you usually have what appears to be random banter with the hosts. For me, this is the best part of the show. In some cases, it's even better than the actual show.

It also sets the tone for how the show will go. On the close to 300 podcasts I have done (~270 of which as a host), the “before-we-hit-record” part makes or breaks the show.

This is top of mind for me because I’m going on podcasts to promote my book, The Male Friendship Experience, and it got me thinking about something that I feel is the hallmark of male friendships—those moments in between.

The Seemingly Random Moments of Nothingness

The reason the "before-we-hit-record” moments are so magical is that there is no performance going on. You are literally trying to get a sense of who the guest is and see if you might connect. It’s like watching an episode of Seinfeld. Things are going on, but it seems to be a show about nothing, and that’s what the in-between moments are all about.

Don’t get me wrong. A podcast episode can capture that. Most podcasts that entertain and educate can capture those in-between moments before you hit record, but some of them build their whole show around it. This is especially true for comedy podcasts like Bad Friends.

It’s More Than a Bit

Bobby Lee and Andrew Santino have known each other for years. There is nothing fake about their banter or friendship underneath the show, but as professional comedians, the show is polished into punchlines, pacing, and callbacks of some of their funniest and worst moments in life. They have a real bond, and that’s why it works so well. Yes, it’s a bit extreme and always chasing the punchline, but guests and staff genuinely enjoy themselves.

Andrew Schulz’s Flagrant is similar in that it’s comedy but with more of a guys hanging out in a lounge type of vibe. The regulars often bust each other's chops, but the overall tone is more learning and hanging out than put-downs. The guests are more eclectic, the topics more broad, and the vibe, while comfortable, can be confrontational.

Both of these show male friendship in a fun, locker-room, bust-my-chops kinda vibe, which is real and entertaining yet is only part of the story.

Deep Dive Into the Bro Science

On the other side, you have got the data/Bro Science pods. Chris Williamson’s Modern Wisdom is the best of these types. Male connection gets more studied (among other things). Things are broken down into frameworks. Loneliness statistics are reviewed. Concepts like attachment theory are discussed. There are real insights being discussed. The rapport with guests and recurring guests feels real, especially the Rabbit Hole episodes where it’s a bunch of guys jaw-jacking about seemingly random stuff—some of which is downright nutty, like the Uber Eats to OnlyFans pipeline.

article continues after advertisement

Each one of these types of shows is legitimate. Neither one is lying to you. Both types show what male friendship is like when an audience is laughing or taking notes. They have in-between moments because that’s part of the show. What is hard for them to show is the experience when the cameras are not rolling, which is what I always loved about doing podcasts.

Before We Hit Record

That phrase is something I have said and heard often. It’s the in-between that gives you a true sense of what the recorded show is going to be like. I got to experience this firsthand recently, being on two podcasts that, while not the big audience of the ones above, were a closer glimpse into friendships between men.

#1 Podcast for People is one of those shows that’s truly the definition of the in-between. Its hosts, Gator and Sliceburg, are good friends who work together at a pizza place in Gainesville, FL, called Satchel’s (Gator owns it).

The absolute randomness of this podcast truly shows what two guys (and field reports from listeners) are doing as they go about their day. When I mean go about their day, I mean the random school pickups, travel on airplanes, and road trips that make up the in-between of friendship and connection. It’s close to if Seinfeld were based in Florida at a pizza parlor with artwork everywhere.

Equally insightful is 3 Dimensional Dads, hosted by Jay, Derrick, and Ian, three dads who love nerding out on Star Wars, video games, and everything in the Marvel universe. While different in tone and tenor (they talk about the benefits of therapy and their struggles), it's another glimpse into three good friends supporting each other.

Even how all of them met is the classic in-between moment. Jay and Derrick met at a midnight screening of "Star Wars: Episode III" (back in 2005) because they both got there early. While waiting around for the show to start, Jay, who was sitting behind Derrick, quips, “I hope this doesn’t suck.” To which Derrick replied, “Me too.” Ian found Derrick and Jay through his wife as she was walking their dog, Leia, and running into Jay’s wife walking their dog, Spidey. Obviously, with dog names like that, their husbands had to meet. Talk about random in-between moments.

article continues after advertisement

It’s About Showing Up, Day After Day

All of these podcasts demonstrate something that’s critical to maintaining a friendship—showing up to someplace where someone will miss you if you’re not there. It’s this combination of regular interactions and the in-between that creates the ties that bond men. If you listen to these shows, yes, you’ll find some deep and difficult conversations, but what you’ll find more is friends caring about each other by dealing with the joy, sorrows, and absurdity of life. That seems to be the secret to lasting male friendships.

item.title: Why Your Therapist Thanks You
item.description:
Relationships

Why Your Therapist Thanks You

Personal Perspective: This is why I so appreciate clients, and I bet your therapist does, too.

Posted September 7, 2026

Source: NoSystem Images / Getty Images Signature

It’s a not-so-well-kept secret. Therapists are nosy. Maybe not all therapists, but c’mon. Who would want to go into a profession where you listen all day to other people’s problems, secrets, quandaries, and so forth? Nosy people. Sure, we want to help you, absolutely. But lots of people want to help others and don’t become therapists. Those people (after a socially acceptable number of minutes of other people going on about personal problems) say, “Dude, you should really go talk to somebody about that.” Therapists can’t say that. They are the somebody.

Over the therapist years, I learned so much more than my nosiness and desire to help others ever suggested I might. And I owe that to all my clients. Thank you, each and every one.

  • Thank you for making me keep learning, all the time. Whenever you had a problem, it wasn’t that it became my problem, but if I didn’t know about it, I wanted to learn. From reading studies that taught me—for instance—that couples might feel better about each other from discussing movies about other relationships or from writing briefly about a problem from the other person’s perspective; from learning about the scourge and trauma of conversion therapy to really understanding manic episodes, you kept me learning. And learning and learning. That’s one of my favorite things in life. So thank you.
  • Thank you for teaching me that all people have “bad” thoughts, but most people are good. Most of us are what we would call “in the range of normal” (remember the bell curve), even when depressed, anxious, bipolar, what have you. But most people don’t think they are normal. From feeling “evil” about wanting to hurt your ex- or boss or even your child: These thoughts are normal. It’s not what you think that makes you a better or worse human; it’s what you do. All of us have “bad” thoughts. Thoughts in themselves are not good or bad; they’re just human. Hopefully, I was able to pay this forward and help lots of clients accept their thoughts and themselves, warts and all.
  • Thank you for increasing my patience. I never really had any. I’ve been in a rush my whole life. It’s bad. I need to slow down, and I’m working on it. Being a therapist helped. It helped me wait. And listen. And listen more. I might have talked too much, but hopefully about helpful things. Therapy takes the time it takes for that person, that trauma, that issue, that decision. Waiting patiently for change and growth to occur at its peculiar pace is a life lesson I take everywhere. Priceless.
  • Thank you for making me a better person, better parent, better partner—in all my relationships. All that listening involved hearing what worked for other people, not just what didn’t. What worked in marriage might not work at a job. What worked in parenting (so kids still talk to you and act like they love you) might not work with a spouse. I learned how people dealt with infuriation without exploding. I learned how humans did things well, and even well-er. So many things. I use them in my own life (without divulging how I learned!). Eternally grateful.
  • Thank you for allowing me to screw up, learn how to apologize, and repair. All therapists blow it. OK, I don’t know that for sure, but therapists are human (AI ones, though having some benefit, blow it for sure). I made mistakes I still think about. I even called people back to apologize. For having a bad day and being snippy. For a tiny part of me wondering if what they said was true. For judging them on their choices. I apologized and told them I was wrong. I hope they forgave me. I may never know. My missteps and attempts at repair schooled me not to judge others on one bad day, one bad behavior, or one bad comment—in or out of the office. Who knows what someone might be going through, anytime, anywhere? A huge gift.
  • Thank you for giving me a place to go and do something useful when my own life was crumbling. I don’t love it, but I also don’t keep it secret: I’ve been married and divorced three times. Those choices are on me, and I gained four incredible children in the process. One of those kids has high-needs autism (and all kids are high-needs when you think about it, right?). Sometimes, it was a lot. Some days were just, well, horrible. With restraining orders and traumatized kids and stress up the yin yang and beyond (yes, thank goodness, I had my own incredible therapist through it all). At first I didn’t know how I might help anyone else on a day my own life was falling miserably apart. Guess what? Going to the office and seeing you was an absolute blessing. A reprieve, a gift. To set aside and know, for a few hours, I could lay down the burden and even use it (or not) in service to help others. Amazing.
  • Thank you for the love. I worked—and still work—to deserve it. I cared deeply about the people I knew as clients, or I couldn’t have done a good job. In fact, I loved many. It was a pleasure and a privilege. There are infinitely more gifts I take with me than I have room for on this list. Hopefully, something I learned from you I also paid forward, so something you taught me may have helped countless others, too. You gave so much, more than you know. I hope I helped, healed, and held a safe space for you. Thank you, ever, ever so much.

item.title: Can We Make Social Media Feel a Little Quieter?
item.description:
Social Media

Can We Make Social Media Feel a Little Quieter?

Five ways I'm protecting my peace online.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • You can find a way of being online that works for you.
  • Boredom isn’t a problem; it gives you space to hear your own thoughts.
  • You don’t have to be on social media simply because you think you should.
Source: Gilles Lambert / Unsplash

Last week, I went on social media for the first time in three months. This was The Summer Experiment I wrote about earlier, when I decided to go off social media. Eight weeks in, I was still loving it. Now the three months were up, and I wanted to find out how it would feel to go back.

I logged into Instagram, my main social media platform. I checked my messages, replied to a few comments, and posted something about my summer offline. And then I promptly logged out again. Why? Because I did not feel good being back there, even if it was just for 15 minutes.

The highlight reels, influencer brand partnerships, and random sponsored posts I never asked to see were all suddenly in my face. It felt so... noisy. Look at me! Look at this! Have you thought about this? Buy this! Every post seemed to be shouting for my attention. Frankly, it made me feel a little sick to my stomach.

I remember the old Instagram, when my feed was mostly friends, beautiful photography, and words from people whose work I enjoyed. Now there are stories and reels and videos and music and advertisements and suggested posts and things the algorithm has decided I might like. It feels so chaotic and out of control. Granted, I'm guilty of having done all of those things in the past, too, mainly because I thought that’s what I should do. But I'm finally realizing why I’ve always resisted it so much.

I’m an introvert who needs a lot of quiet. I love living in the countryside surrounded by greenery. I find busy cities overwhelming. Too much noise, too many people, and too much visual stimulation can leave me feeling frazzled. I’ve always preferred the quiet company of animals to crowds of people. Maybe my temperament simply means I need a quieter way of being online.

I’m not blind to the positives of the online world. You can find meaningful communities, make genuine friendships, find inspiration, and learn from people with expertise. But it takes work to get the positives to outweigh the negatives. So, if I do go back properly, these are the boundaries I want to put in place:

  1. Keep the bedroom screen-free. Firstly, my sleep is sacred to me, and research has linked nighttime digital use with poorer sleep. That’s reason enough for me to keep my bedroom offline. Secondly, I want the final things I see at night and the first things I see in the morning to be the things I have deliberately chosen, not whatever the algorithm has decided to serve me. A book, my husband, my dog, and the view from our bedroom window.
  2. Protect the first and last 30 minutes of your day. The start and end of your day are too precious to hand over to a screen. Start and end your day by connecting with yourself or the immediate world around you. Journal, meditate, stretch, read, drink your coffee slowly, or simply see what your own mind comes up with before you invite the whole world into it. Don’t let the algorithm influence the mood you’re going to start the day on. Don’t fill your head with other people’s lives before you’ve even had a chance to inhabit your own.
  3. Kill boredom scrolling. This was the big one for me. During my experiment, I realized that even when I wasn’t scrolling social media, I tried to find other ways to scroll. The news, the weather, online shopping. Anything, really. Once I stopped doing that, I discovered that boredom isn’t a problem. You can just sit there. You can daydream, pick up a magazine, look through a coffee-table book, or go sit outside. You might even be surprised by what your brain comes up with when you stop feeding it things. I was.
  4. Curate your feed. If I return, I want to be more intentional about what I allow into my feed. If someone consistently leaves you feeling inspired, informed, or happy, great. If they make you feel anxious, inadequate, or exhausted, goodbye. And if you’re following someone for expert advice, make sure they actually have the expertise to give it. Consume only what you choose to consume.
  5. Remember that you’re allowed to take breaks, or even leave. This might be the biggest thing I’ve learnt. I spent years thinking I should be on social media because I’m an author. I thought I needed to be visible, promote my books, connect with readers, and keep up with what everyone else was doing. But three months away taught me something freeing: I don’t actually have to be there. I can decide whether to be there and how to be there. I can find a simpler, quieter way of using it for my work. Or I can take another break. Or I can leave.
article continues after advertisement

Three months ago, I thought this experiment was going to prove that I could live without social media. And it did. But more importantly, it also reminded me that I really like quiet. That I like daydreaming and doodling. That I like going for a walk and coming home without having documented it. That I like discovering what everyone else is up to by talking to them, not by following their socials. And, perhaps most importantly, I like having enough space in my own head to hear what I truly think.

item.title: Your Office Romance Isn’t Just Between Two People
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Your Office Romance Isn’t Just Between Two People

When two coworkers fall for each other, the whole team feels it.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Workplace romances can change how coworkers interpret trust, loyalty, and influence.
  • Even fair decisions may look questionable when one partner has more power at work.
  • Coworkers may communicate less openly when they fear information will travel between partners.

Two colleagues start dating. They keep things professional: No flirting in meetings, no obvious favoritism, and no change in performance. From their perspective, nothing at work has really changed.

Everyone else may see it differently.

Workplace romance is usually perceived as a private decision between two adults. Advice focuses on whether the couple should tell HR, if they should keep the relationship private, or what might happen if they break up. These are reasonable concerns, but they overlook something important: A workplace romance also changes how other people interpret the social environment around them.

The third party in a workplace romance

Research by Rebecca Chory and Hailey Gillen Hoke found that people involved in workplace romances tended to underestimate how negatively coworkers perceived the relationship. The gap was especially noticeable when the relationship involved people at different levels of the organizational hierarchy.

So while a couple can genuinely believe they are behaving professionally, their coworkers may subtly change how they interact with them.

Imagine that Maria and Daniel work on the same team. Before they start dating, another colleague might feel comfortable telling Maria, “Daniel really mishandled that client meeting.” Once everyone knows Maria and Daniel are together, a comment like this becomes more complicated. Will Maria tell Daniel? Will Daniel take it personally? Will criticizing one partner affect that colleague’s relationship with the other?

Maria does not actually have to repeat the conversation for the dynamic to change. The possibility that information might travel differently can be enough to make coworkers more cautious.

Chory and Hoke found that when coworkers attributed career-related motives to a workplace romance, trust declined. That lower trust was associated with less honest and less accurate communication with the people involved.

In other words, a relationship does not need to create an actual conflict of interest to create uncertainty about one.

Romance can redraw the invisible map of the office

Every workplace has an informal social map. Employees learn who is close to the boss, who shares information with whom, who can influence a decision, and who can be trusted with a complaint that should go no further.

None of this appears on an organizational chart, but people still pay close attention to it because it helps them navigate the workplace.

An office romance can redraw that map. Two people who were previously viewed as separate actors may now be seen as a pair. Information shared with one may be assumed to reach the other. A disagreement with one may feel as though it could affect someone's relationship with them both.

This becomes especially sensitive when one partner has more organizational power.

Suppose a manager begins dating someone in the same department. A few months later, that employee receives a high-profile assignment. The employee may have fully earned it. The manager may not have been involved in the decision at all. But coworkers now have another explanation available to them.

That creates a problem of attribution.

Fairness at work depends partly on whether decisions are actually fair. But it also depends on whether employees believe they understand why those decisions were made. Once romance becomes part of the picture, success can be harder for others to interpret.

When success becomes harder to explain

Research on hierarchical workplace romance shows just how complicated this can become. Suzanne Chan-Serafin and colleagues found that lower-status employees who were romantically involved with someone higher in the organizational hierarchy could face career penalties. Evaluators were less willing to promote them and less willing to select them for training opportunities than comparable employees who were not involved in such relationships.

There is an uncomfortable irony here. People often assume that dating someone powerful gives an employee an unfair career advantage. Yet the perception of that advantage may itself damage the employee’s reputation.

Other research has found that judgments about workplace romance also vary by gender, age, industry, and management status. Chory, Lisa Mainiero, and Sean Horan found that workplace romances were generally viewed as more damaging to women’s careers than men’s. They also found substantial differences between industries in how comfortable people were with workplace romance and how much reputational damage they associated with it.

The person presumed to benefit from the relationship may therefore also be incurring a professional cost. Every legitimate success can be followed by the uncomfortable question: Would this have happened if they were not dating?

Why coworkers gossip

This may help explain why workplace romances generate so much gossip.

It's tempting to dismiss office gossip as simple nosiness, and sometimes it is. But gossip can also be a way for employees to make sense of uncertainty in their social environment.

Seep Sethi and Shalini Srivastava found a positive association between workplace romance and workplace gossip in a study of hotel employees. Co-workers may speculate: If two colleagues are dating, does one now have access to information through the other? Are they likely to support each other in disagreements? Is it still safe to speak candidly in front of either one? Could one partner’s preferences influence the other’s decisions?

Seen this way, office-romance gossip can be about more than romance. Fellow employees may be trying to understand their organization’s informal structure of trust and influence.

“But we keep it professional”

Couples often respond to these concerns by saying that they keep their relationship separate from work. And many probably do. The difficulty is that their professionalism does not determine how others interpret their relationship. A couple controls its own behavior, but cannot fully control the assumptions coworkers make about information sharing, loyalty, or favoritism.

Workplace romance is not inherently harmful. Some research has found positive associations between workplace romance, engagement, psychological well-being, and job performance. Having a supportive partner who understands your daily work experience may make your job considerably more enjoyable.

The problem is that what benefits a couple may still create uncertainty for the colleagues around them.

For this reason, the most important boundary a couple in a workplace romance must consider is not hiding their affection but protecting the independence of their professional decisions. When employees are romantically involved, particularly when one has greater authority, they should think carefully about whether either could influence the other’s evaluation, promotion, pay, workload, scheduling, or access to opportunities. An employee should not automatically gain access to confidential workplace conversations simply because they share a relationship with a supervisor outside the office.

There is nothing particularly surprising about people falling in love at work. Workplaces bring people together around shared goals, interests, pressures, and experiences. But workplaces are also social systems. Employees continually monitor relationships to understand where trust, information, and influence lie.

An office romance may belong to two people emotionally but at work, it rarely affects only those two.

item.title: A Ghost in the Machine: An Eerie Tale from the Psych Lab
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

A Ghost in the Machine: An Eerie Tale from the Psych Lab

Personal Perspective: An early research experience and overcoming adversity.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • A project in the psychology lab gets torpedoed in a most weird and mysterious way.
  • How to overcome a research calamity with resilience and humility.
  • The lessons learned have positive, cascading effects lasting decades.

This column’s general theme is finding the extraordinary in everyday life. It’s not always easy, especially when bad things happen. But sometimes very bad things can become very good things in the most unexpected ways. To illustrate this point, I’ll recount an event from my undergraduate days that became a major learning moment in both my personal and professional lives. For better or worse, you’ll also get a glimpse at how research sausage can be made.

The Incident

This was back when polygraphs had rows of ink pens drawing jiggly lines on slow-moving paper rolls. I’d just turned 21 and was running my first experiment, the most crucial part of my honors thesis project. I painstakingly ran one subject at a time. Each was nestled into a soft reclining chair with unobtrusive electrodes taped to their arms and hands to detect reactions to what they watched on TV. So far, I had data from about 20 of a planned 80 subjects. The results were looking great, with the polygraph lines jiggling pretty much as predicted.

That’s when it all came crashing down. I stared in horror at the output emerging from the polygraph. Actually, it looked perfectly normal, but that was the problem: I was running an equipment check, and no subject was in the chair.

What I was seeing was impossible, more séance than science. I looked back and forth between the polygraph beside me and the empty chair on the other side of the one-way mirror. Whose responses am I recording? And how can they look so good?

The Background

It’s the start of my senior year at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. I’d done nearly all my major requirements, and I wanted to graduate in December to save money. It was a stressful time. I undertook honors projects in both psychology and sociology (I never could decide between them); took a full course load; bussed tables at a local restaurant; worked on grad school applications; and tried to maintain some semblance of a life.

I designed the experiment with my honors advisor, the great Seymour Sy Berger. It involved a weird, relatively unexplored phenomenon called motor mimicry. Sy found that, under certain conditions, people imperceptibly and unconsciously imitate others’ physical actions.

My study measured subjects’ skin conductance, heart rate, and electromyographic (EMG) responses. EMG captures the intensity of muscular nerve impulses, which would indicate mimicry if it lights up for the right muscles at the right times during the video.

The Ghost Hunt

Doubting our polygraph was occupied by spirits, Sy and I first replicated the haunting. We played the video and checked our readings against my earlier printout by placing one atop the other and shining a light through the back. (Very scientific!) They were identical.

Superimposing the “ghost” printout and a real human subject’s also revealed near-identical EMGs. That was a major clue that the electrodes were picking up a non-human electrical source. If not a ghost, perhaps the big black-and-white TV was the culprit. We tried moving it away from the subject’s chair.

article continues after advertisement

Our demon was exorcised! The highly sensitive electromyographic electrodes had been picking up the electron beam sprayed by the TV’s cathode ray gun. Old TVs worked by shooting electrons into the phosphor coating on the back of the screen and, apparently, beyond as well.

We also discovered that the EMG measure was affected by changes in the contrast of the on-screen images. Unfortunately, those contrast changes coincided with moments when subjects were predicted to respond to the video. That's why the first wave of data looked so good. Of course, that data set was worthless. Worse, I had no hope of re-running the experiment in time to graduate at the end of the semester.

The research, planning, equipment set-up, and completed sessions were all for naught. I was crestfallen.

The Silver Linings

Grasping at straws, I thought of retitling my thesis to “How My Honors Project Was Murdered by a Cathode Ray Gun.” But Sy had a better idea: A redesigned experiment. It required a new video presentation, but only half the subjects originally planned—40 instead of 80.

I remade the video and was up and running the next week.

Here are some results:

  1. I developed an even deeper appreciation for the wisdom of mentors.
  2. I learned more than I ever wanted to know about cathode ray guns and televisions.
  3. The EMG results weren’t quite up to snuff statistically, but I finished the project and graduated with honors.
  4. That helped me win a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation—a coveted golden ticket to any grad school in the country.
  5. I chose Stanford’s Ph.D. program in sociology. There, I received fantastic training in statistics, among other topics.
  6. Using my new statistical skills, I took a fresh look at my old thesis data as a side project. As I suspected, the EMG data were badly skewed—a common problem but easy to fix. Upon de-skewing, the results clearly supported the original hypotheses.
  7. I reconnected with Sy; we wrote up a report, and the first journal we sent it to published it. This became my first professional paper.
  8. I’d learned skills and attitudes that contributed greatly to my Ph.D. thesis project and my next publication.
  9. These publications helped secure my first faculty position.
  10. Many years later, my position led to this platform and recounting the story.

Had things gone differently my senior year, I’d have realized only too late that my 80 identical EMG readouts were garbage. I wouldn’t have had the problem-solving experience with my mentor, and my remarkably satisfying graduate school experience and professional career might never have unfolded as they did.

article continues after advertisement

In a very real sense, I owe it all to the ghost in the machine.

item.title: Postpartum Depression Has a Thousand Faces. A Mother May Meet Several
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Postpartum Depression Has a Thousand Faces. A Mother May Meet Several

With postpartum depression, the people trying to help may be listening for the wrong face

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum depression can change its form over the course of a single illness.
  • It can feel like fear, grief, overwhelm, or guilt about asking for help.
  • A listener or a therapist who expects only sadness can miss fear, shame, irritability, or grief.

One insight I have shared for many years with medical students, psychiatry residents, and young psychotherapists is deceptively simple: the disorders we name in our diagnostic systems have many faces.

We know, of course, that one person’s depression is not another person’s depression. But there is something else we sometimes forget: One person’s depression is not always even the same depression. During the course of suffering, depression may change its face, its language, its logic, and even the story it tells the person who is living with it.

I have learned this particularly from mothers who have spoken with me about postpartum depression.

For one mother, it may become a kind of gaslighting algorithm: My brain plays games with me. It takes a beautiful video of my smiling baby and somehow tags it “Danger,” “Trap,” and “Lifelong Mistake.” The frightening part is that, for a moment, I believe the tags and every time I feel ashamed and guilty.

Later, the same depression may become grief for a ghost: I am not grieving my baby. I am grieving the mother I thought I would be—the woman who existed so clearly in my imagination but somehow never arrived. It feels as if I am supposed to be different women whom I never met.

At another moment, it may feel like sensory overdose: Forget sadness or guilt. Everything is too loud, too close, too demanding. My body feels as though it has nowhere left to hide. And every dark corner where I choose to hide exposes me more than before.

And sometimes it becomes a zero-sum game: If I take an hour for therapy, I am taking an hour from my baby. If I need medication, I have failed. If I take medication, I am poisoning my baby, If I need help, someone else must pay for my weakness.

These are not different diagnoses but different faces of the same suffering.

And so a therapist who listens only for “sadness” may miss fear, shame, or guilt. A partner looking for tears may miss the confusion and irritability. A physician asking whether she loves her baby may miss the unbearable grief she feels for the mother she believed she was supposed to become.

Properly understanding postpartum depression may need to include the question, “What face is it wearing today?”

Once we understand this, we may start to understand a mother who deals with, or talks about, her experience with PPD.

item.title: The Limited and Lopsided Vision of Bullying
item.description:
Bullying

The Limited and Lopsided Vision of Bullying

Neuroscientists strive to see with a more balanced and holistic perspective.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Bullies harness the brain's left hemisphere that lacks care or empathy for others.
  • The narrow focus of the brain's left hemisphere cuts us off from a sense of connection to Others.
  • Using a two-eyed, dual brain-hemisphere approach expands our vision and insight.

Bullying done from one person to another parallels bullying done from one populace to another. Person-to-person abuse is the microcosm. Populace-to-populace bullying, as we see in colonialism where the settlers abused the Indigenous population, acts as a macrocosm. Settlers oppressing and harming Indigenous populations occurs in colonialism. All of these forms of bullying require a pronounced lack of empathy.

Bullying puts on blinders to Others' knowledge, experience, humanity, and personhood. It does not walk in the Other’s shoes, does not feel their pain, and does not see through their eyes. It is biased in favour of its own tunnel vision. In recent years, neuroscientists have begun to see the limits of this approach.

When we examine the bullying mindset while keeping brain science in mind, we can see that bullying—both micro and macro—compares to experiencing the world through only one brain hemisphere while ignoring data from the brain’s other hemisphere. It produces a lopsided, unbalanced, and limiting point of view, which is exactly what scientific studies strive to avoid.

Our left and right brain hemispheres are different

Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist researches brain lateralization—the different ways in which our left and right brain hemispheres see and connect with Others and the world itself. As he describes it, our brains construct reality “from two incompatible world views.” The left is defined by narrow self-focus, whereas the right experiences profound connection with Others. The left is like an opportunist, while the right compares to an altruist.

In his book The Master and His Emissary, McGilchrist expresses concern with the normalizing of abuse culture where the left hemisphere dominates, creating an unhealthy, unsustainable world of callous exploitation. He explains that harmful behaviours may originate in damaged right-brain function:

"There is also a direct correlation between sadness and empathy, on the one hand, and feelings of guilt, shame and responsibility, on the other. Psychopaths who have no sense of guilt, shame or responsibility, have deficits in the right frontal lobe, particularly the right ventromedial and orbitofrontal cortex."

In contrast to the empathic and emotional deficits of the opportunist left hemisphere, McGilchrist characterizes the altruist right side of the brain as paying “attention to the Other, whatever it is that exists apart from ourselves, with which it sees itself in profound relation. It is deeply attracted to, and given life by, the relationship, the betweenness, that exists with this Other.” The single-minded focus of the bully gives way to a brain hemisphere that privileges connectivity with Otherness.

McGilchrist identifies the left brain’s “need to influence and manipulate,” which is an apt description of what bullies strive to accomplish. McGilchrist says the left’s focus is on “individual self-belief,” which forms a sharp contrast to the expansive bonding and empathy that occur via the right hemisphere. The left objectifies and exploits while the right connects and bonds.

Accessing the altruistic right hemisphere through Indigenous knowledge

Another way to characterize the division of the human brain is as the left hemisphere being correlated with a Western perspective, while the right hemisphere is correlated with an Indigenous viewpoint. The settlers escaped from scarcity, suffering, and trauma. Not to excuse it, but they appear to have harnessed the left-brain opportunist approach that McGilchrist sees as focused on “grasping, getting, and feeding.”

In contrast, the Indigenous peoples existed with abundance and experienced their world with a sense of deep connection. Their mindset, grounded in empathy and bonding for all living things—imbued with spirit—parallels the right hemisphere’s approach. The settlers were desperately focused on needs, while the Indigenous impacted by them were imbued with a sense of self as part of a rich natural whole. It was a tragic clash.

Neuroscientists are engaging with Indigenous knowledge

Melissa Perreault, a Métis professor in neuroscience, acknowledges that limiting brain research to left-sided Western methods “to the exclusion of others is a failure.” She is part of a group formed by the Canadian Brain Research Strategy that engages with Indigenous Knowledge holders who have research interests in the brain and mental health.

As outlined recently in an article in the Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences, when neuroscientists factor in Indigenous ways of experiencing reality, it sounds like they want to balance the left hemisphere’s Western view with the Indigenous right hemisphere’s connection to the world:

"Connectivity, which has emerged as an important theme in systems level neuroscience, actually builds upon Indigenous knowledge that everything in the universe is connected, whether it is the connection between ancestral spirits and the mortal world; the connection between the water, the land, and the animals that live there; and the connections between individuals and the environment."

Bullying, abusing, exploiting—whether from person to person or populace to populace—are the opposites of this right-brain connectivity that informs Indigenous culture. As McGilchrist states, “the left hemisphere view is designed to aid you in grabbing stuff. Its purpose is utility and its evolutionary adaptation lies in the service of grasping and massing ‘things.’” He associates this kind of impulse with the “decline of civilization.”

Replacing bullying’s cyclops with Two-Eyed Seeing

In Homer’s Odyssey, the cyclops is a one-eyed bully who traps Odysseus and his men with the goal of destroying and consuming them. It is a terrifying but accurate depiction of much colonialist harm done to Indigenous peoples. It is a mythical version of McGilchrist’s left-brain descriptor focused on “getting, grasping, and feeding.”

While McGilchrist worries about our Western, colonialist, bullying ways that he sees as the “unopposed action of a dysfunctional left hemisphere,” an international team of neuroscientists is opening up and listening to the right brain’s perspective as conveyed through Indigenous peoples and culture. It’s a hopeful antidote to today’s toxicity.

In the Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences, the new path forward is described as “Two-Eyed Seeing,” which is “a guiding principle that was conceived by Mi'kmaw Elder Albert Marshall in 2004.” Seeing with both eyes, like seeing via both brain hemispheres, is the opposite of the one-eyed cyclops’ bullying view. Its goal is an integration of “Indigenous and Western perspectives represented without domination or assimilation.”
